paragraphs.source_en: The low chronology is undermined by the fact that in cases of the superimposition of clearly definable styles, the Pastoral style lies over the Round Head style and therefore later. In several cases brightly coloured Pastoral cattle are depicted over faded Round Head compositions. The archaeological record also suggests that painting was practised before the advent of domestication. At Uan Afuda cave in the Acacus ten excavated grinding stones bear traces of red and yellow colours, and a wooden spatula with traces of red ochre was dated to 8,790 BP. Since the shelter presents several Round Head paintings, Di Lernia (1999) discusses the relationship between the excavated coloured objects and the rock art present in the shelter and hypothesizes that they were possibly created by Mesolithic groups.

paragraphs.source_en: From 1990 to 1996, during the Tadrart Acacus missions directed by Mori, a few samples of coloured rock were taken to obtain direct dating of rock art. The samples came from the shelters of Lancusi, T-Afozzigiart, A-Fozzigiart and Tin Torha North and the direct dating was achieved by accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) measurements obtained from a small quantity of organic matter, consisting of charcoal or other pigments or binder constituents extracted from the painted surface (Ponti & Sinibaldi 2005). The majority of dated paintings were of the Pastoral style and only two of them were probably of the Round Head style. At T-Afozzigiart the sample was taken inside the painted area containing vague outlines of a probable animal with small circles filled in with white colour.

paragraphs.source_en: This pattern frequently occurs in Round Head paintings but the direct dating result at 5,360+50 BP (calBP 6,146±95) is quite recent. At A-Fozzigiart typical Round Head red human figures outlined in white, superimposed on an unclear white figure with small red circles, were dated to 5,580+210 BP (calBP 6,379±240) (Ponti&Sinibaldi 2005; Mori et al. 2006). Such late dates of the Round Head style may either support the low chronology or indicate that this artistic tradition in the Acacus had a much longer duration than generally believed. As for the Tassili Plateau, samples of Round Head paintings have been taken from Sefar, Tin Tazarift and Tan Zoumaitak in 2008-2009 for AMS dating, but the results have not yet been published (Hachid et al. 2010).
